title: How Que Alicea Built an Environmental Firm in a Male-Dominated Industry
guestBio: Que Alicea is the founder and CEO of Q & A Consulting LLC, a San Francisco environmental compliance and safety firm specializing in hazardous materials testing, air quality assessments, and construction compliance across California and Nevada. A former medical day spa owner and paramedical aesthetician, she pivoted into industrial hygiene after a disaster recovery job changed the course of her career. She is a 2026 Enterprising Women of the Year Award recipient, 2025 WRMSDC Supplier of the Year, and 2025 Asian Inc Entrepreneurial Champion of the Year.
excerpt: Que Alicea never planned to start an environmental firm — she took a disaster recovery job to fund her spa and accidentally built an award-winning company. In this episode, she gets real about navigating male-dominated job sites, surviving the self-funded early days, and why relationships win contracts, not certifications.
metaDescription: Que Alicea built an award-winning environmental firm with no business plan. Hear how she navigated male-dominated job sites and won contracts as a women-owned business.
keyTakeaways: Businesses don't always begin with a polished plan — sometimes the most powerful thing you can do is walk through the open door in front of you.
Confidence on a job site, a boardroom, or any room where you're outnumbered starts with knowing your material so thoroughly that no one can take the conversation away from you.
Overhead doesn't pause while clients pay late — building a financial cushion for the gap between net-30 invoices and actual payroll is a non-negotiable survival skill for early-stage businesses.
Women-owned business certifications like WBENC can put you on a shorter list, but it's the relationships you invest in — touch point by touch point — that ultimately win the contract.
Every interaction with a client, partner, or peer is a deposit into a relationship account; treat it that way and the returns will compound over time.
Hiring experts in the areas where you're weakest — rather than trying to master everything yourself — is one of the most powerful growth moves a founder can make.
Building a business purely for the money is a fragile foundation; sustainable entrepreneurship is rooted in purpose, passion, and a reason to get up and fight on the hard days.

quiz.title: What Kind of Entrepreneur Are You Building Toward?
quiz.description: Que Alicea didn't plan to become a CEO — she just kept saying yes to the next right thing. This quiz will help you discover your entrepreneurial edge: the instinct, strength, or season that's shaping the way you build. There are no wrong answers. Every path leads somewhere powerful.

A.name: The Door-Walker
A.description: You don't wait for a perfect plan — you move when the opportunity shows up and figure out the details as you go. You trust your gut more than a spreadsheet, and your greatest breakthroughs have come from saying yes before you felt fully ready. The challenge for you is learning to build systems that support the momentum you create. This episode is your reminder that some of the most successful companies were born from exactly that kind of instinct.

B.name: The Technical Authority
B.description: You lead with expertise, and your confidence comes from knowing your material cold. You've earned your place at the table through deep preparation, and you know that speaking with precision is one of the most powerful tools you have. Your challenge is learning to let relationships carry as much weight as credentials. This episode will show you exactly how one woman used both to build something undeniable.

C.name: The Relationship Builder
C.description: You understand intuitively that business is personal — that every touch point is a deposit and every genuine connection is an asset. You invest in people before you ever need anything from them, and your network reflects that long-term thinking. Your challenge is making sure you're also building the financial and operational backbone to match your relational strengths. This episode will affirm your instincts and give you a framework to grow from.

D.name: The Purpose-Driven Founder
D.description: You're not in this for the money — you're in it for the mission, the impact, and the reason to get up on the hard days. You think in decades, not quarters, and you're building something you'd be proud of even if no one handed you an award for it. Your challenge is translating that deep purpose into the tactical decisions that keep the lights on. This episode will speak directly to the fire in you and give it somewhere practical to go.

options.text: Stop waiting for the perfect plan. The door won't stay open forever.
Go deeper on your expertise earlier — that knowledge will be your armor.

Make sure your 'why' is strong enough to carry you through the years, not just the launch.

content:
What does it look like to build a business you never planned to start, in an industry where almost no one looks like you? For Que Alicea, founder and CEO of Q & A Consulting LLC, it looked like renting equipment she couldn't yet afford to buy, waiting on net-45 invoices with payroll already due, and walking onto job sites where people instinctively turned to her male project manager before they ever acknowledged her. It looked like doing it anyway.

In this episode of The Manage Her® Podcast, Aimee sits down with Que for an Entrepreneur Spotlight conversation that is equal parts business school and permission slip. If you've ever wondered whether you have enough experience, enough credibility, or enough of a plan to build something of your own — this episode is going to shake something loose in you.

The Accidental Pivot That Changed Everything

Que's story doesn't start with a vision board or a business plan. It starts with a medical day spa she owned, a cash-flow gap, and a disaster recovery job she took to fill it. That short-term gig introduced her to the world of industrial hygiene — the science of identifying and controlling workplace environmental hazards — and she found, almost to her own surprise, that it wasn't so different from the paramedical skincare work she already knew. Both fields are rooted in how environmental exposure affects the human body. The science connected. The door was open. She walked through it.

What began as contract work quietly became a company. Q & A Consulting LLC now specializes in hazardous materials testing — asbestos, lead, mold, PCBs — air quality assessments, and compliance work for construction and infrastructure projects across California and Nevada. The name, by the way, was never her initials. It was a placeholder that stuck. Sometimes the accidental details become the permanent ones.

What It Actually Feels Like to Be the Only Woman in the Room

Que doesn't sugarcoat the reality of being a woman — and a woman of color — in a heavily male-dominated field. She's walked onto job sites where the crew's first instinct is to direct questions to her male project manager, not to her. She knows that feeling. And she's learned exactly how to handle it: speak technical.

When you demonstrate that you know your material cold — the specific tests, the regulatory standards, the science behind the work — you earn the room's attention in a way that no title alone can. That kind of confidence isn't arrogance. It's preparation meeting presence. It's the armor you build when you study hard enough that doubt doesn't have a foothold.

But Que also gets honest about the moments that armor gets heavy. Doubting yourself is real. Wondering whether you belong is real. The answer she's landed on is simple but not easy: trust what you know. You did the work. You earned the expertise. You don't need anyone's permission to own the room.

The Unglamorous Truth About the Early Days

If you've been romanticizing entrepreneurship, Que's early-days chapter will re-calibrate you — not to discourage you, but to prepare you. The self-funded reality of building Q & A Consulting meant paying for lab fees and renting expensive field equipment before revenue was consistent. It meant watching a net-30 payment agreement quietly become net-45 while payroll stayed stubbornly on schedule. Overhead is due whether your clients pay on time or not. That gap is where a lot of businesses quietly break down, and Que navigated it by planning for it rather than hoping it wouldn't happen.

The turning point — the moment the firm felt real — came when Q & A Consulting landed a contract at San Francisco International Airport. Landing SFO wasn't just a revenue milestone. It was a signal. It told Que, and the market, that the firm could compete and win at the highest levels. Those anchor moments matter. They become the stories you tell yourself on the hard days when you're not sure you're building something that will last.

Certification, Relationships, and the Truth About What Actually Wins Contracts

Que holds WBENC certification as a women-owned business, and she's clear-eyed about what it does and doesn't do for you. Certification puts you on a shorter list. It opens doors that would otherwise stay closed. But it does not hand you a signed contract. The contract comes from the relationship — from the consistency, the follow-through, and the genuine investment in the people you're trying to serve.

She describes client relationships the way you might describe dating: every touch point is a deposit. The check-in text. The Sunday blessing. The congratulatory message when a client's project gets funded. None of it is transactional. All of it is intentional. And over time, those deposits compound into the kind of trust that makes you the obvious call when an opportunity opens up.

The WBEC community also gave Que something invaluable beyond certification: access to other women who were building things, asking hard questions, and willing to be honest about what was working and what wasn't. That's where she first heard the advice that changed how she thought about hiring: hire up. Bring in the experts instead of trying to become one in every area. Your job as the CEO is to lead the vision, not to master every technical function within it.

Why You Don't Build Something Real for the Money

One of the most honest moments in this conversation comes when Que talks about why she kept going — through the late payments, the job site slights, the solo years before the team grew. It wasn't the money. It was the reason to wake up. The mission. The thing that made the hard days feel worth it instead of just hard.

Entrepreneurship built for pure profit is fragile. When the profit is slow, or delayed, or redirected back into the business, you need something more durable to stand on. Purpose is more durable. A vision for what you're building — and who it's for — is more durable. Que built something that will outlast any single contract, any single award, any single difficult year. And she did it without a business plan, without a bank loan, and without waiting until she felt ready.

If you're sitting on an idea, waiting for more credentials or more certainty or more of something you can't quite name — this episode is your sign. The door doesn't stay open forever. Walk through it.
